beats.beat: The company operates in two segments: creation of infrastructure, and operating a ready-mix concrete (RMC) plant at Kashimira, Thane district, Maharashtra.

Its product lines are railways (designing and constructing platforms, station buildings, gauge conversion and laying railway tracks), bridges (beam, cantilever, arch, suspension, cable-stayed and truss bridges) and roads (bituminous and concrete roads).

Work is won through tenders: a client floats a tender, a pre-bid meeting is held, the contractor bids, the lowest quote receives the Letter of Acceptance, the contractor deposits a performance guarantee, and only then is the site handed over for execution.

Major customers include Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority, Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation, plus private clients.
Concentration is a defining feature: top customers made up 57% of revenue in FY2018, and Western Railway alone is 52% of the order book and has been a client since 2006.
The filing's claimed strengths are an experienced team with 20-plus years in infrastructure, the box-pushing technique, a state-of-the-art RMC facility and a 'healthy order book'.
The filing's own SWOT lists weaknesses: the slow pace of government projects and the risk that a working-capital crunch may affect profitability.

beats.beat: The clearest trend is falling revenue: ₹86.61 crore in FY2014, ₹90.21 crore in FY2015, ₹74.53 crore in FY2016, ₹73.44 crore in FY2017 and ₹60.53 crore in FY2018.
Net profit after adjustments: ₹0.96 crore in FY2014, ₹0.78 crore in FY2015, ₹0.33 crore in FY2016, ₹0.16 crore in FY2017 and ₹3.15 crore in FY2018 — a sharp jump at the end of a falling revenue line.
Profit before interest, depreciation and tax: ₹7.84 crore in FY2014, ₹9.46 crore in FY2015, ₹7.83 crore in FY2016, ₹6.76 crore in FY2017 and ₹9.29 crore in FY2018.

Borrowings tell the working-capital story: long-term borrowings fell from ₹5.87 crore in FY2014 to ₹1.33 crore in FY2018, while short-term borrowings rose from ₹30.82 crore to ₹35.37 crore. Total assets moved from ₹70.62 crore to ₹82.32 crore.

The filing warns of negative cash flow in recent years and discloses ₹405.02 lakh of unsecured loans repayable on demand as at March 31, 2018 — a demand from lenders could hurt cash flow and financial condition.
The read-across: this is a small revenue base carrying heavy short-term debt, which makes the FY2018 profit jump the most important number — it is the base against which the issue will be priced.

beats.beat: The promoter is Amit Bholanath Mishra, also Managing Director; he holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of the pre-issue paid-up equity share capital.
Three other directors — Bharat Kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — each hold 300 equity shares, listed as whole-time directors.
Key management personnel include CFO Anchal Pachori, aged 28 and a Chartered Accountant, and Company Secretary Mohit Soni, aged 26; Hatim Sakerwala separately holds 9% of the company's equity.

Related-party transactions disclosed for FY2018 include a loan taken of ₹68.4 lakh from KMP/board members, director remuneration of ₹57.7 lakh, and outstanding related-party payables of ₹324.3 lakh as at March 31, 2018.

Governance flags in the filing: no independent agency appraised the project; no monitoring agency exists; two promoter-promoted companies, Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited, were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation; and equity shares were issued in the last 12 months at a price that may be lower than the issue price.

On one axis the record is clean: none of the directors is on the RBI list of wilful defaulters, no criminal cases have been filed against the directors, and the promoter has not been declared a wilful defaulter.

beats.beat: India's infrastructure sector includes power, bridges, dams, roads and urban infrastructure; the filing calls construction a highly fragmented and working-capital-intensive market contributing roughly 8% to India's GDP.

Growth evidence cited in the filing: the eight core industries grew 4.2% in 2017-18, the logistics sector was expected to grow at a 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020, and India's GDP growth was expected to stay above 7% in 2017.

Demand drivers named by the company: government flagship programmes including Smart Cities, AMRUT, Make in India and Power for All; eased FDI norms in 15 sectors including real estate and construction; and rising industrialisation, urbanisation, disposable income and population growth.
Competition is not quantified in the excerpts: the filing says the company operates in a competitive industry with competitors in both the organised and unorganised sectors, but names no rivals.
Headwinds the filing acknowledges include the slow pace of government projects, changes in government policies, and the ever-present working-capital crunch.
The regulatory landscape the filing surveys includes the Companies Act, 2013, GST, the Factories Act, 1948 and environmental legislation such as the Water and Air Pollution Acts.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-based civil infrastructure contractor: it builds railway platforms, bridges and roads, mostly for government clients, and runs a ready-mix concrete plant. Its DRHP shows a company with a concentrated customer base and heavy working-capital needs going public on the SME board.
The offer is 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a price to be determined; the company says the money will be used for working capital and general corporate purposes.
The biggest relationship is Western Railway, a client since 2006, which accounts for 52% of orders on hand; the top customers as a group were 57% of revenue in FY2018.

The financial story is a falling top line with a recent profit jump: revenue fell from ₹90.21 crore in FY2015 to ₹60.53 crore in FY2018, while PAT jumped to ₹3.15 crore in FY2018 from ₹0.16 crore in FY2017.

intro.purpose: Orient the reader in plain language: who the company is, what it does, what it is raising and why it matters.

beats.beat: The offer comprises 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at an issue price to be determined. The excerpts do not reproduce an explicit 'Fresh Issue' label and name no offer-for-sale seller; the disclosed use of proceeds points to the money going to the company.
The lead manager to the issue is Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited and the registrar is Bigshare Services Private Limited.
Use of proceeds has two disclosed objects: ₹1,130 lakhs (₹11.30 crore) for working capital requirements, and general corporate purposes, the amount of which is not disclosed in the excerpts.

Two process flags appear in the filing: the company has not appointed any independent agency to appraise the project, and no monitoring agency has been appointed — deployment of funds is at the discretion of management and the board, monitored by the audit committee.

beats.beat: Customer concentration: Indian Railways — through Western Railway — was 57% of revenue in FY2018 and 52% of orders on hand; the loss of that customer would cause a significant dip in revenue.
Tender dependence: revenue depends on winning government and PSU bids; if bids fail or contracts are cancelled, suspended or adjusted, the order book is not necessarily indicative of future revenue.

Working-capital strain: the company had negative cash flow in recent years, short-term borrowings of ₹35.37 crore at FY2018, and ₹405.02 lakh of unsecured demand loans; delayed recovery of receivables would hurt financial condition.
Geographic concentration: most revenue comes from operations in and around Mumbai; adverse developments affecting that region would directly hit revenue and results.

Governance and process risk: the working-capital project has no independent appraisal and no monitoring agency — only audit-committee oversight — while the promoter's two earlier companies were struck off in 2016 and general litigation is pending.
